e-21585.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent to a Trajectory Given an Initial Value Problem
e-21585.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068149/assets/d8be54eddd0358742170a03b3c55e0cb94eaf2a7d59f12e1c4361a6197d29847.png)
Consider the initial value problem and its solution given above. What is the tangent vector to the solution curve at the point corresponding to $t=\ln 2?$
e-21585.worked_solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

First, we compute the point that corresponds to $t=\ln 2$ on the given trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & ={e}^{3(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+2{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =8[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+2\cdot 2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =8[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 8\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation of our system, we obtain the tangent vector to the trajectory.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}12 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2(12)+1(4) \\ 1(12)+2(4)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}24+4 \\ 12+8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}28 \\ 20\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

e-21586.knowledge_point: Finding Nullclines of a System of Differential Equation
e-21586.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t)-y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)-y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. Find equations of the $x$- and $y$-nullclines for the corresponding phase space.
e-21586.worked_solution:
Recall that: 

- The $x$-nullcline is a line for which $x' = 0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are vertical). So, to find it, we set the first equation of the system equal to $0{:}$

$$
3x-y=0 
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
y = 3x
$$

- The $y$-nullcline is a line for which $y' = 0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are horizontal). So, to find it, we set the second equation of the system equal to $0{:}$

$$
-2x-y=0 
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
y = -2x
$$

Plotting these in the phase space, we obtain the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068149/assets/66cdd05ac68d762c5b78df40b22f9e0cd660099c13e48e9eb71c81c73a044280.png)

e-21588.problem:
A sketch of the phase space with nullclines and the corresponding direction field of tangents to the solutions of a system of differential equations is shown below (the tangents are not drawn to scale). Sketch the trajectory of the solution starting at the marked point.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068149/assets/0cf7942e618f0465ead5b98c6404a3747e505db75517725971c833c97121ab64.png)
e-21588.worked_solution:
Let's sketch the trajectory.

- We start at the given point, moving along with the flow (downward and slightly to the right) until the trajectory intersects the $x$-nullcline, where the tangents are vertical.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068149/assets/105bdbdcac5f0ff20f71a0131bf5bb3cbafe0e93ce8bc733a51c2dcb3fb8364f.png)

- Next, the flow continues downward, but the trajectory starts to turn slightly to the left.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068149/assets/96757a3aee3b161b2ba9887cd85f977f063807779604647dd791cf265790cabc.png)

- After that, the trajectory continues to go downwards and slightly to the left to infinity.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068149/assets/658c15d2291368d0e6836ba19b90157d49dee4a510d58cddf7f85ddc9ff72a8d.png)

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+4y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above and its trajectory passing through the point $(-1,2)$ in the phase space of the system. What is the tangent vector to the trajectory at this point?
after.worked_solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

In our case, the trajectory (solution) passes through the point $(x,y)=(-1,2)$ in the phase space. Substituting the coordinates of this point into the equations of our system, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} & =-3x+y \\  & =-3(-1)+2 \\  & =3+2 \\  & =5 \\ {y}^{′} & =2x+4y \\  & =2(-1)+4(2) \\  & =-2+8 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent vector to the trajectory is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} \\ {y}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

In our case, the trajectory (solution) passes through the point $(x,y)=(-1,2)$ in the phase space. Substituting the coordinates of this point into the equations of our system, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} & =-3x+y \\  & =-3(-1)+2 \\  & =3+2 \\  & =5 \\ {y}^{′} & =2x+4y \\  & =2(-1)+4(2) \\  & =-2+8 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent vector to the trajectory is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} \\ {y}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t)-2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4x(t)+y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above and its trajectory passing through the point $(0,-2)$ in the phase space of the system. What is the tangent vector to the trajectory at this point?
after.worked_solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

In our case, the trajectory (solution) passes through the point $(x,y)=(0,-2)$ in the phase space. Substituting the coordinates of this point into the equations of our system, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} & =3x-2y \\  & =3(0)-2(-2) \\  & =0+4 \\  & =4 \\ {y}^{′} & =-4x+y \\  & =-4(0)+(-2) \\  & =0-2 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent vector to the trajectory is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} \\ {y}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

decision.explanation: At t=ln(3), x(t)=(3·3^(-2),2·3)=(1/3,6). Applying the system matrix gives x′(t)=(-2/3,6), which is option c.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,x(t)={e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the initial value problem and its solution given above. What is the tangent vector to the solution curve at the point corresponding to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡3?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

First, we compute the point that corresponds to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ on the given trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & ={e}^{-2(\operatorname{ln}⁡3)}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation of our system, we obtain the tangent vector to the trajectory.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2(\frac{1}{3})+0(6) \\ 0(\frac{1}{3})+1(6)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3} \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

x′(t)=[−2001]x(t),x(0)=[32],x(t)=e−2t[30]+et[02] Consider the initial value problem and its solution given above. What is the tangent vector to the solution curve at the point corresponding to t=ln⁡3?

d
[6−23]

EXPLANATION

Recall that the xy-coordinate plane is called the phase plane of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a trajectory (or orbit).

First, we compute the point that corresponds to t=ln⁡3 on the given trajectory:

x(ln⁡3)=e−2(ln⁡3)[30]+eln⁡3[02]=19[30]+3[02]=[130]+[06]=[136]

Substituting this into the equation of our system, we obtain the tangent vector to the trajectory.

x′(ln⁡3)=[−2001][136]=[−2(13)+0(6)0(13)+1(6)]=[−236]

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms x(ln 3)=(1/3,6). Applying the system matrix gives the tangent vector (-2/3,6), option c. Option b gives the position rather than the derivative.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent to a Trajectory Given an Initial Value Problem
content.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,x(t)={e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the initial value problem and its solution given above. What is the tangent vector to the solution curve at the point corresponding to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡3?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

First, we compute the point that corresponds to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ on the given trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & ={e}^{-2(\operatorname{ln}⁡3)}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation of our system, we obtain the tangent vector to the trajectory.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2(\frac{1}{3})+0(6) \\ 0(\frac{1}{3})+1(6)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3} \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above and its trajectory passing through the point $(-1,-2)$ in the phase space of the system. What is the tangent vector to the trajectory at this point?
after.worked_solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

In our case, the trajectory (solution) passes through the point $(x,y)=(-1,-2)$ in the phase space. Substituting the coordinates of this point into the equations of our system, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} & =2x+y \\  & =2(-1)+(-2) \\  & =-2-2 \\  & =-4 \\ {y}^{′} & =-x+3y \\  & =-(-1)+3(-2) \\  & =1-6 \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent vector to the trajectory is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} \\ {y}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

after.html:
Question 5
?

{x′(t)=2x(t)+y(t)y′(t)=−x(t)+3y(t) Consider the system of linear differential equations above and its trajectory passing through the point (−1,−2) in the phase space of the system. What is the tangent vector to the trajectory at this point?

a
[−1−2]
b
[−23]
c
[−4−5]
d
[45]
e
[21]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the xy-coordinate plane is called the phase plane of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a trajectory (or orbit).

In our case, the trajectory (solution) passes through the point (x,y)=(−1,−2) in the phase space. Substituting the coordinates of this point into the equations of our system, we obtain the following:

x′=2x+y=2(−1)+(−2)=−2−2=−4y′=−x+3y=−(−1)+3(−2)=1−6=−5

Therefore, the tangent vector to the trajectory is [x′y′]=[−4−5].

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent to a Trajectory Given an Initial Value Problem
content.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above and its trajectory passing through the point $(-1,-2)$ in the phase space of the system. What is the tangent vector to the trajectory at this point?
content.worked_solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

In our case, the trajectory (solution) passes through the point $(x,y)=(-1,-2)$ in the phase space. Substituting the coordinates of this point into the equations of our system, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} & =2x+y \\  & =2(-1)+(-2) \\  & =-2-2 \\  & =-4 \\ {y}^{′} & =-x+3y \\  & =-(-1)+3(-2) \\  & =1-6 \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent vector to the trajectory is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} \\ {y}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)-y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)-3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. Find equations of the $x$- and $y$-nullclines for the corresponding phase space.$\,$
The $x$-nullcline is $y=$ {{field-1}}. 

$\,$
The $y$-nullcline is $y=$ {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
Recall that: 

- The $x$-nullcline is a line for which ${x}^{′}=0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are vertical). So, to find it, we set the first equation of the system equal to $0:$

$$
2x-y=0\,⇒\,y=2x
$$

- The $y$-nullcline is a line for which ${y}^{′}=0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are horizontal). So, to find it, we set the second equation of the system equal to $0:$

$$
-x-3y=0\,⇒\,y=-\frac{1}{3}x
$$

Plotting these in the phase space, we obtain the following:

content.knowledge_point: Finding Nullclines of a System of Differential Equation
content.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4x(t)+y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. Find equations of the $x$- and $y$-nullclines for the corresponding phase space.
$\,$
The $x$-nullcline is $y=$ {{field-1}}. 

$\,$
The $y$-nullcline is $y=$ {{field-2}}.
content.worked_solution:
Recall that: 

- The $x$-nullcline is a line for which ${x}^{′}=0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are vertical). So, to find it, we set the first equation of the system equal to $0:$

$$
x+y=0\,⇒\,y=-x
$$

- The $y$-nullcline is a line for which ${y}^{′}=0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are horizontal). So, to find it, we set the second equation of the system equal to $0:$

$$
-4x+y=0\,⇒\,y=4x
$$

Plotting these in the phase space, we obtain the following:

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)-3y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4x(t)+y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. Find equations of the $x$- and $y$-nullclines for the corresponding phase space.
$\,$
The $x$-nullcline is $y=$ {{field-1}}. 

$\,$
The $y$-nullcline is $y=$ {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
Recall that: 

- The $x$-nullcline is a line for which ${x}^{′}=0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are vertical). So, to find it, we set the first equation of the system equal to $0:$

$$
x-3y=0\,⇒\,y=\frac{1}{3}x
$$

- The $y$-nullcline is a line for which ${y}^{′}=0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are horizontal). So, to find it, we set the second equation of the system equal to $0:$

$$
4x+y=0\,⇒\,y=-4x
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding Nullclines of a System of Differential Equation
content.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=5x(t)+y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. Find equations of the $x$- and $y$-nullclines for the corresponding phase space.$\,$
The $x$-nullcline is $y=$ {{field-1}}. 

$\,$
The $y$-nullcline is $y=$ {{field-2}}.
content.worked_solution:
Recall that: 

- The $x$-nullcline is a line for which ${x}^{′}=0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are vertical). So, to find it, we set the first equation of the system equal to $0:$

$$
-3x+y=0\,⇒\,y=3x
$$

- The $y$-nullcline is a line for which ${y}^{′}=0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are horizontal). So, to find it, we set the second equation of the system equal to $0:$

$$
5x+y=0\,⇒\,y=-5x
$$

Plotting these in the phase space, we obtain the following:

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-4x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. Find equations of the $x$- and $y$-nullclines for the corresponding phase space.
$\,$
The $x$-nullcline is $y=$ {{field-1}}. 

$\,$
The $y$-nullcline is $y=$ {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
Recall that: 

- The $x$-nullcline is a line for which ${x}^{′}=0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are vertical). So, to find it, we set the first equation of the system equal to $0:$

$$
-4x+y=0\,⇒\,y=4x
$$

- The $y$-nullcline is a line for which ${y}^{′}=0$ (i.e., the tangents to trajectories are horizontal). So, to find it, we set the second equation of the system equal to $0:$

$$
2x+2y=0\,⇒\,y=-x
$$
